blocks.text: Imagine you're a software engineer testing whether a new algorithm improves processing speed. How do you decide if the observed improvement is real or just due to random chance?

blocks.markdown: Hypothesis testing is a statistical method used to make decisions about a population based on sample data. It helps us determine if an observed effect is statistically significant or if it could have occurred by random chance.

blocks.title: Null and Alternative Hypotheses
blocks.text: The null hypothesis ($H_0$) is a statement that there is no effect or difference. The alternative hypothesis ($H_1$ or $H_a$) is the statement that there is an effect or difference.

blocks.markdown: To begin hypothesis testing, we first formulate the null and alternative hypotheses. The null hypothesis often represents a default position or a statement of no change, while the alternative hypothesis represents the outcome we want to test for.

blocks.title: Formulating Hypotheses
blocks.prompt: A company claims that their new battery lasts longer than 10 hours on average. Formulate the null and alternative hypotheses.

steps.text: Identify the parameter of interest, which is the average battery life.

blocks.answer: The null hypothesis is $H_0: \mu = 10$ hours, and the alternative hypothesis is $H_1: \mu > 10$ hours.

blocks.title: Test Statistic
blocks.text: A test statistic is a standardized value that is calculated from sample data during a hypothesis test. It is used to determine whether to reject the null hypothesis.

blocks.markdown: Once hypotheses are formulated, we compute a test statistic from the sample data. This statistic helps us decide whether the sample provides enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis.

blocks.caption: Z-test statistic formula, where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean, $\mu_0$ is the population mean under $H_0$, $\sigma$ is the population standard deviation, and $n$ is the sample size.

blocks.title: Calculating a Test Statistic
blocks.prompt: A sample of 30 batteries has a mean life of 10.5 hours with a standard deviation of 1.2 hours. Test the hypothesis that the mean battery life is 10 hours using a Z-test.

steps.text: Identify the sample mean $\bar{x} = 10.5$, population mean $\mu_0 = 10$, standard deviation $\sigma = 1.2$, and sample size $n = 30$.
Compute the test statistic using the formula: $z = \frac{10.5 - 10}{\frac{1.2}{\sqrt{30}}}$.

blocks.title: Interpreting the p-value
blocks.text: The p-value is the probability of observing a test statistic as extreme as, or more extreme than, the observed value under the null hypothesis. A small p-value indicates strong evidence against the null hypothesis.

blocks.markdown: After computing the test statistic, we determine the p-value. This value helps us decide whether to reject the null hypothesis. Typically, a p-value less than 0.05 is considered statistically significant.

blocks.title: Type I and Type II Errors
blocks.text: A Type I error occurs when we incorrectly reject a true null hypothesis. A Type II error occurs when we fail to reject a false null hypothesis.

blocks.markdown: Understanding errors in hypothesis testing is crucial. A Type I error is controlled by the significance level (often 0.05), while the probability of a Type II error is related to the power of the test.

points: Formulate null and alternative hypotheses based on the research question.
Compute a test statistic and interpret the p-value to make decisions.
Understand and distinguish between Type I and Type II errors.
